result.summary: The Greeks bury Machaon and Nireus while Nestor consoles Podaleirius, and Eurypylus nearly destroys the Greek camp. Odysseus and Diomede fetch Achilles' son Neoptolemus from Scyros, parting him from his mother Deidameia. He arrives at Troy in his father's arms, routs the Trojans from the wall and is feasted by the Greeks.

scenes.title: Burial of Machaon and Nireus
scenes.summary: The Greeks bury Nireus and Machaon under one mound.

scenes.title: Nestor consoles Podaleirius
scenes.summary: Podaleirius wants to die at his brother's tomb. Nestor speaks of shared sorrow and Fate, and leads him away.
scenes.stakes: Podaleirius may take his own life from grief.

scenes.title: Eurypylus assaults the ships
scenes.summary: Eurypylus slays Peneleos and many Greeks and drives them behind their wall. Athena heartens them, then a truce for burial is held.
scenes.stakes: The Greek ships and army face destruction.

scenes.title: Odysseus asks Neoptolemus to come
scenes.summary: Odysseus and Diomede find Neoptolemus on Scyros and offer him his father's arms and a bride. He agrees; Deidameia fears for him.
scenes.stakes: Deidameia fears losing her son as she lost her husband.

scenes.title: Farewell to Deidameia
scenes.summary: Deidameia pleads, Lycomedes warns of the sea, and Neoptolemus departs for the ship.
scenes.stakes: A mother's grief at parting; the young hero risks war and sea.

scenes.title: Voyage to Troy
scenes.summary: The ship sails with fair wind past Troad landmarks as the heroes tell Neoptolemus of Achilles.

scenes.title: Neoptolemus defends the wall
scenes.summary: Armed in Achilles' gear, Neoptolemus drives Eurypylus' men from the wall with Athena's aid.
scenes.stakes: The Greek ships and camp could be burned and the army slain.

scenes.title: Praise, feast and Achilles' tent
scenes.summary: Neoptolemus kills Celtus and Eubius. Phoenix weeps over him, the Greeks feast and honour him, and he mourns in his father's tent.

notable_quotes.reason: Concise statement of the mortal lot.
Neoptolemus in Achilles' arms seems Achilles himself.

analysis.text: Grief and consolation run through the book, in Podaleirius and Deidameia, set against the hero's eagerness for glory.
Neoptolemus inherits his father's arms and fame, renewing Greek hopes.

fun_facts.text: The poem is by Quintus of Smyrna, a later Greek epic poet, and continues the Iliad.

language_notes.text: "Without the ships" means outside the ships' camp; "Argives" is another name for the Greeks.
"Goodlihead" is an archaic word for beauty or comeliness.
"Twain" means two; the two men are Machaon and Nireus.
"Essayed" means tried or attempted.
"Ravined up" means devoured greedily; the body was consumed on the funeral pyre.
"On the knees of Gods" echoes Homeric phrasing: the outcome of events rests with the gods.
Machaon's father was Asclepius, god of healing, so Nestor expects him to win a place among the gods.
Hercules fought the Centaurs near Pholoe, a mountain in Arcadia, after they attacked him over wine at the centaur Pholus' cave.
Eurypylus is Hercules' grandson: his father Telephus was Hercules' son, so Hercules' ghostly terror aids his descendant.
"Haft" appears to be an odd word here, perhaps for hail; it is listed with snow and sleet as winter weather.
Ceteians are Eurypylus' Mysian followers, named from the river Cetius; here they fight beside the Trojans.
"Embassage" means an embassy, a delegation sent to ask for a truce.
A "barrow" is a burial mound of earth heaped over the dead.
"Twain" is an archaic word for "two"; here Odysseus and Diomede.
"Reverent eyes of awe": they look at him with awed respect because he resembles his father Achilles so closely.
"Tydeus' warrior son" is Diomede, identified by his father. Odysseus oddly names himself last, in the third person.
"Achaean" and "Danaans" are Homeric names for the Greeks.
The shield's scenes of earth, heaven and sea recall the shield Hephaestus made for Achilles in the Iliad.
"Bare back ... his corse": carried his body back to the ships. Odysseus and Ajax defended Achilles' body.
Menelaus' daughter is Hermione; she is offered as a bride. "Hellas" means Greece.
Odysseus and Diomede had earlier come to Scyros and persuaded Achilles to join the Trojan war, where he died.
Ilium is another name for Troy; 'fount of tears' calls it a spring of sorrow.
Achilles was killed at Troy; Deidameia blames Odysseus and the Greek leaders, who now draw her son into the same war.
Removing landmarks means moving boundary stones to seize a widow's land, a recognized wrong in ancient societies.
Weird means fate or destiny.
Lycomedes describes dangerous sailing seasons by stars: the Archer (Sagittarius), the Goat (Capricorn) and Orion's setting, all in late autumn and winter.
The Pleiads are a star cluster whose setting in late autumn marked the start of stormy seas.
Raven-haired, the Lord of all the sea, is Poseidon, called by a dark-haired epithet.
Levin-flame is lightning.
Hawsers are thick mooring ropes; "anchor-stones" are heavy stones used as anchors in ancient ships.
"Sea-queen's lord" is a periphrasis for Poseidon (the Greek name; this translation does not use it here), husband of the sea-goddess Amphitrite; he is the sea-god who grants the fair voyage.
"Hard-bestead" means hard pressed, in great difficulty.
"Aweless" means fearless, not inspiring awe in the modern sense; "fain" means eager.
"Laertes' seed" is Ulysses, son of Laertes; "Aeacus' son" is Achilles' father's line, here meaning Achilles, grandson of Aeacus, whose tomb stands at Sigeum.
Protesilaus was the first Greek to die at Troy, leaping ashore first. Legend says elms by his tomb wither at the sight of Troy, then sprout again.
Tydeus' strong son is Diomede, an Argive leader, here spotting the assault on the Greek wall.
"Change of armour" means spare sets of armour hung in the tent, some Odysseus' own, some taken from dead comrades.
Socus was a Trojan ally whom Odysseus killed in the Iliad; his armour is now given to Diomede.
"Pelian" refers to the great ash spear from Mount Pelion, which was Achilles' and is now his son's.
"Kine" means cattle; "steading" is a farmstead.
"Aweless" in this translation means fearless, not awe-inspiring.
"Ness" means a headland; Sigeum is the promontory near Troy.
"Aeacid" means descendant of Aeacus, Achilles' grandfather, so Neoptolemus is the Aeacid's son.
Scion means offspring or descendant; Meges is described as the son of Dymas, and the dead youths are his sons.
The Fates 'span a thread' alludes to the Fates spinning each person's lifespan; a brief thread means a short life.
Peleides means 'son of Peleus', a name for Achilles; Neoptolemus is his son and so resembles him.
Telephus' son is Eurypylus. His 'wretched sire' Telephus was once wounded by Achilles' spear, so Phoenix implies Neoptolemus will surpass him too.
'Had fain' means he would gladly have; he wished to rush out at once but night stopped him.
Aeacid means descendant of Aeacus: Achilles was Aeacus's grandson, so Neoptolemus is his great-grandson.

context_notes.text: Podaleirius and Machaon were brothers, sons of Asclepius and physicians of the Greek army.
Nestor's son Antilochus was killed defending his father in the Trojan War.
Hades is the god of the dead and the name of the underworld.
Eurypylus, son of Telephus, leads the Mysians to aid Troy after Achilles' death. The War-god is Ares.
Athena (Minerva) favors the Greeks and often intervenes to restore their courage in battle.
Burying or burning the dead during a truce was a regular custom in Homeric-style war.
Scyros is an Aegean island where Achilles' son Neoptolemus was raised by his mother Deidameia and her father's household.
Hephaestus was the divine smith of the gods, who made Achilles' armour.
Thetis, a sea-goddess, was Achilles' mother. His armour was awarded to Odysseus after his death.
Neoptolemus is leaving Scyros for Troy with Odysseus, to take up his dead father Achilles' place.
Lycomedes is king of Scyros, Deidameia's father, and grandfather of Neoptolemus, Achilles' son.
Thetis, a sea-goddess, was Achilles' mother; the Nereids are her sister sea-nymphs. They rejoice for her grandson.
Deidameia is Neoptolemus' mother, whom Achilles loved on Scyros; she stays behind while her son goes to war.
Ida is the mountain range near Troy; Chrysa and Smintheus' temple honor Apollo, whose epithet Smintheus is tied to the region.
Neoptolemus is Achilles' son, newly arrived at Troy and wearing his father's armour for the first time.
Hephaestus, the divine smith, made Achilles' armour; it fits Neoptolemus miraculously.
Eurypylus leads the Ceteians, allies of Troy who have been pressing the Greeks hard.
Pallas is Athena, protector of the Greeks, who intervenes here to aid Neoptolemus.
Phoenix was Achilles' aged tutor and companion, who raised him from infancy, so he is moved by Neoptolemus' likeness.
Achilles' furious return to battle after Patroclus was killed is the famous event of the Iliad.
Briseis was Achilles' captive concubine, whose seizure by Agamemnon caused his quarrel in the Iliad.

literary_notes.text: Nireus is compared to the Deathless Ones in beauty, setting up the contrast with his weak fighting.
Podaleirius' fasting in dust and thoughts of suicide show the depth of his devotion to his brother.
Nestor appeals to manly restraint, showing his role as a traditional elder counsellor.
Fate is given hands and a careless will, hurling good and evil from Olympus.
Good and evil gifts are likened to things blown about by gusts of wind, showing the randomness of fate.
Eurypylus is likened to Ares, stressing his frenzied, unstoppable violence.
Comparing Eurypylus to Hercules slaughtering Centaurs makes the Greeks seem like powerful but doomed foes, and hints at his ancestry.
A flooding river wrecking banks and cliffs conveys Eurypylus' overwhelming, destructive force as Greek ranks collapse.
Goats sheltering from a storm extend the earlier image, showing the Greeks as timid and cowering behind their wall.
Strife is pictured as a being who does not sleep, showing the war cannot rest.
Deidameia's grief-wasted body is compared to snow melting under sun and east wind, conveying slow, steady wasting away.
The sound of the surrounding sea lulling the island contrasts with Deidameia's sleeplessness in the next sentence.
Her dread that her son will go to war and bring more grief hints at the sorrow to come.
Her wail is likened to a cow lowing for her lost calf, with echoing hills matching the echoing hall.
Neoptolemus is compared to a spirited horse held back by its rider, showing his eagerness and his mother's pride.
Deidameia's grief is compared to a swallow circling her nest after a serpent has eaten her young.
Comparing him to a radiant star suggests his brilliance and a destiny beyond the ordinary.
Likening him to Ares, the War-god, gives him terrifying splendor and shows he inherits his father's martial nature.
Her heart melting like lead or wax over coals conveys slow, consuming grief through a homely image.
The narrator turns to a general truth about mothers, universalizing Deidameia's anxiety.
The sail "melted" in sea-haze, echoing the earlier melting of Deidameia's heart and linking her loss with the ship's departure.
Ulysses' tact in hiding Achilles' tomb shows his discretion and care, matching his epithet "discreet of soul."
The elms "discern" Troy and wither, as if grieving; the image evokes the doom attached to the war.
The claim that he seemed Achilles himself stresses the son's resemblance to his father and prepares the Trojans' fear.
Storm-bound sailors longing for a fair wind compare to the Greeks' relief at Neoptolemus' arrival.
A lion defending its cubs from hunters shows Neoptolemus' fury, with the Greek camp as the cubs.
Eurypylus boasts of victory while the narrator reveals that death approaches him from Neoptolemus' hand.
Children cowering at thunder show the Trojans' helpless terror, with Neoptolemus as Zeus' storm.
The torrent rushing at men on a narrow path conveys the Trojans' trapped dread.
Fish lured by firelight and speared depict Trojans drawn to destruction by Neoptolemus.
Missiles falling like snowflakes on rock show the divine armour's invulnerability.
Vivid, violent detail of the stone crashing through helmet and skull conveys Neoptolemus' savage strength.
Emotions are 'tides' sweeping over Phoenix, showing joy and grief surging in turn.
Achilles is likened to a strong sapling growing fast, expressing his rapid growth and Phoenix's nurturing care.
Night rises from the ocean in a dark robe, giving the evening a bodily, ceremonial presence.
The lion's whelp in the empty den mirrors Neoptolemus in his dead father's tent, conveying grief and inheritance.
